metadata.title: AICR Introduction
metadata.audience: Northeastern researchers and students about to use the AICR GPU cluster for the first time; assumes no other film or book

skin_warnings: BIDEA: palette=claude but the cold open is 'BrutalistHesitantWriter' — COLD OPEN LAW wants ClaudeComposerAsk

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. AICR is not the cluster where you build and test your AI work. It's the cluster where you run the big jobs. It's a shared GPU cluster for AI research in Massachusetts, and this lecture covers what it is, how you get on, where your files live, and how you run a job.

show.event: types 'AICR is the cluster where I build and test my AI work'
backspaces 'build and test' -> 'run the big jobs for'

props.text:

build and test my AI work

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the newcomer's framing (build and test) and corrects it to the real one (run the big jobs).

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. An HPC cluster: many computers wired together and shared by many people. A GPU: a chip that does AI math far faster than a normal processor. Slurm: the scheduler. You ask for resources, and it decides when you run. A partition: a named group of machines with its own rules. A PI: the principal investigator, the faculty member who leads a project. And Open OnDemand: a website that gives you the cluster in a browser.

beats.narration_text: Start with what it is. AICR stands for AI Compute Resource. Six universities at the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center, together with the Massachusetts AI Hub, built one cluster, and they share it.

beats.narration_text: Inside are two kinds of GPU. Two hundred forty-eight NVIDIA B200s, and one hundred fifty-two RTX PRO 6000s. That's four hundred GPUs in all.

beats.narration_text: Around the GPUs: fast storage, a modern software stack for machine learning, and a CPU-only section for the work that needs no GPU, like cleaning and analysing data.

beats.narration_text: Northeastern already has its own cluster, called Explorer. Treat AICR as an extension of it. You develop and test on Explorer. When the code works, you bring it to AICR for the production run. AICR is shared by every partner university, so it isn't the place to debug.

beats.narration_text: Getting on starts with a faculty member. The principal investigator submits a brief proposal through a request form. Access comes through that project.

beats.narration_text: Once you're on a project, the easiest door is Open OnDemand, at o o d dot A I C R dot A I. It sends you to a sign-in page. You choose your identity provider, then sign in with your Northeastern username and password.

beats.motion_claim: The real sign-in page; the camera pushes in to the identity-provider choice as it is named.

beats.narration_text: One thing changes: your username. On the cluster it's slightly different, so accounts from the partner schools stay distinct. If you're j dot smith on Explorer, you're j underscore smith underscore n e u on AICR.

shot.visual_intent: 'j.smith' in mono under the label Explorer; a copy slides right under the label AICR, its dot turns into an underscore and '_neu' slides on.

beats.narration_text: Your files live in three places, the same three as on Explorer. Home, for small scripts and your environment. Scratch, for temporary output from running jobs. And the project directory, for shared, longer-term work.

shot.visual_intent: Three containers land in a row: a small box (home), a wide open bin (scratch), a cabinet (project); each gets its real path as a label.

beats.narration_text: Home holds a hundred gigabytes. Delete a file there by accident, and you have seven days to recover it. The project directory has the same seven-day safety net.

shot.visual_intent: The home box with '100 GB'; a file page lifts out and vanishes, a seven-day dial sweeps, and the page comes back; the cabinet gets the same dial.
shot.motion_claim: The home box with '100 GB'; a file page lifts out and vanishes, a seven-day dial sweeps, and the page comes back; the cabinet gets the same dial.

beats.narration_text: Scratch is huge. Ten terabytes, and up to fifteen million files. But nothing in scratch can be recovered, and there's a thirty-day purge. So move anything important out before it's gone.

shot.visual_intent: The scratch bin fills with blocks, one marked with a terracotta dot; '10 TB' lands; a thirty-day sweep line crosses the bin; the marked block is lifted out to the cabinet just before the rest vanish.

beats.narration_text: Compute is split into partitions. One is CPU only. Four have GPUs: a batch and a devel partition for the B200s, and a batch and a devel partition for the RTX cards. Every GPU node carries about two point three terabytes of memory.

shot.visual_intent: A drawn table builds row by row from the source: cpu, b200-batch, b200-devel, rtx-batch, rtx-devel, with GPU and max walltime columns.
shot.motion_claim: A drawn table builds row by row from the source: cpu, b200-batch, b200-devel, rtx-batch, rtx-devel, with GPU and max walltime columns.

beats.narration_text: Batch partitions are for jobs you submit and walk away from. They run up to twenty-four hours, and they support more than one GPU. Devel partitions are for interactive work: four hours at most, and four running jobs per user.

shot.visual_intent: Two bars grow side by side: a long one to 24 h (batch) and a short one to 4 h (devel); under devel four job slots fill and a fifth bounces off.
shot.motion_claim: Two bars grow side by side: a long one to 24 h (batch) and a short one to 4 h (devel); under devel four job slots fill and a fifth bounces off.

beats.narration_text: Before you ask for more than one GPU, confirm your code can actually use them. If it can't, the extra cards sit idle.

shot.visual_intent: Four GPU blocks in a row; a job box plugs into all four; only the first lights up and its meter fills, the other three stay dark with empty meters.
shot.motion_claim: Four GPU blocks in a row; a job box plugs into all four; only the first lights up and its meter fills, the other three stay dark with empty meters.

beats.narration_text: And idle is watched. A background process tracks GPU utilization and cancels jobs that sit idle. So end your interactive session when you're done. A tool called jobstats will also report how each job used what it asked for.

shot.visual_intent: A utilization line runs along a time axis, drops to zero and stays flat; a watcher marker reaches it and the job block is struck out and removed; the freed GPU lights for the next job in the queue.

show.event: GPU goes to the next job

shot.motion_claim: A utilization line runs along a time axis, drops to zero and stays flat; a watcher marker reaches it and the job block is struck out and removed; the freed GPU lights for the next job in the queue.

beats.narration_text: You can see the live list yourself. The command s info prints every partition, its time limit, and its node count. Run it and you may see more partitions than the five here, because the cluster keeps changing.

show.event: real partition rows print (captured read-only, 2 October 2026)

beats.motion_claim: The real command and its real output print line by line.

beats.narration_text: AICR runs Slurm, so there are three ways to work. s batch, for jobs that run without you. s run, for an interactive shell. And Open OnDemand, in the browser.

props.title: Three Ways to Work on AICR

beats.motion_claim: Three named routes, each landing as one large library icon as it is spoken.

beats.narration_text: A batch job is a script. The lines that start with S BATCH are your request: which partition, how many CPUs, one GPU, sixteen gigabytes of memory, and a time limit of thirty minutes.

show.event: the script header prints line by line

props.title: myjob.slurm — the request
props.sparkLine: Every #SBATCH line is part of the request.

beats.motion_claim: The real script header from the training material prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Below the request is the work. Clear the loaded modules. Load CUDA and miniforge. Activate your environment. Then run your training script.

show.event: the script body prints line by line

props.title: myjob.slurm — the work
props.code:
module purge
module load cuda/13.1
module load miniforge3/25.3.0-3
source activate myenv

python training.py

beats.motion_claim: The real script body prints line by line.

beats.narration_text: Submit it with s batch and the file name. If your script writes logs into a folder, create that folder first. Then three commands follow the job around. s queue shows your queued and running jobs. s cancel stops one. And s acct shows what a finished job actually used.
beats.motion_claim: The commands from the training material land in order; no output is shown because none was run.

beats.narration_text: For an interactive shell on a GPU node, use s run. This one asks the RTX devel partition for eight CPUs, sixteen gigabytes, and one GPU, for one hour. Always set the time, so the session ends even if you forget. And type exit to give the GPU back.
beats.motion_claim: The real srun command from the training material; exit releases the allocation.

beats.narration_text: Or skip the terminal. Open OnDemand launches graphical sessions, such as JupyterLab or a desktop. You choose the partition, the time, and the resources, and it submits the job to Slurm for you. Those sessions count against the devel limits.

shot.visual_intent: A browser window with three choice chips (partition, time, resources); a job box leaves the window, enters a Slurm queue, and takes one of the four devel slots from B41.
shot.motion_claim: A browser window with three choice chips (partition, time, resources); a job box leaves the window, enters a Slurm queue, and takes one of the four devel slots from B41.

beats.narration_text: To move large data, the primary method is Globus. Northeastern has a subscription. You set up a Globus account with your Northeastern credentials, then connect a folder on Explorer, or on your own machine, to a folder on AICR.

show.event: camera moves down to the account set-up steps; ring

props.caption: Northeastern Research Computing docs, captured 2 October 2026

beats.motion_claim: The real documentation page; the camera moves from the title to the set-up steps as they are described.

beats.narration_text: Last, the part people forget. Accounts and project directories on AICR are temporary. Once a year there's a check-in. The PI renews the request, and the project continues.

shot.visual_intent: A ring of twelve month ticks; a marker travels round it and reaches a gate at the top labelled 'annual review'; a check lands, the gate opens, and the marker starts another lap.
shot.motion_claim: A ring of twelve month ticks; a marker travels round it and reaches a gate at the top labelled 'annual review'; a check lands, the gate opens, and the marker starts another lap.

beats.narration_text: And when the project ends, the data has to leave. AICR is not permanent storage. Move your results back to a Northeastern resource. Questions go to the Research Computing team, at r c help at northeastern dot e d u.

shot.visual_intent: The AICR rack on the right with the project cabinet; its blocks ride the belt back to the Northeastern rack on the left; the cabinet empties and pales; the email address lands underneath.
shot.motion_claim: The AICR rack on the right with the project cabinet; its blocks ride the belt back to the Northeastern rack on the left; the cabinet empties and pales; the email address lands underneath.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. AICR is a shared GPU cluster, with two hundred forty-eight B200s and one hundred fifty-two RTX PRO 6000s. You develop on Explorer, and bring the production run to AICR. A PI's proposal gets you on, and you sign in through Open OnDemand. Home holds a hundred gigabytes. Scratch holds ten terabytes, with a thirty-day purge. Batch partitions run twenty-four hours, devel partitions run four, and idle GPU jobs get cancelled. Projects are reviewed every year, and your data goes home at the end.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I'm about to run my first production job on a shared GPU cluster that uses Slurm. Here is my training setup: [describe it in two sentences]. Write an sbatch script that asks for one GPU and a 30-minute time limit. Then tell me which of my files belong in home, which in scratch, and which in the project directory. Then check two things yourself. Does every S BATCH line ask only for what your code can use? And is anything you can't afford to lose sitting in scratch?
